subject: Mathematics
title: Angles and Shadows: Trigonometry in Daily Life
hook: From measuring temple heights to tracking the sun's angle — trigonometric functions are everywhere.

slides.title: Measuring the School Temple Height
slides.storyContext: Arjun stands 20 meters from a temple and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 45°. Priya says: 'We can find the height without climbing!' Mr. Kapoor, a surveyor, explains: 'This is trigonometry.'

slides.title: Why Trigonometry Matters
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor tells Arjun and Priya: 'Trigonometry built the pyramids. It guides ships across oceans. Architects use it to design buildings. Astronomers use it to measure stars.'

slides.title: Angle Measurement: Degrees and Radians
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor teaches: 'Angles can be measured two ways — degrees (protractor) and radians (mathematical standard).'

points.label: Degree
points.text: 1° = 1/360 of a full rotation. Straight angle = 180°.

points.label: Radian
points.text: 1 radian = angle when arc length = radius. π radians = 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Degrees divide a circle into 360 parts; radians use radius length as the natural unit.

slides.title: Degree vs. Radian: Key Anchors
slides.storyContext: Priya practices conversions using key anchors.
slides.inSimpleWords: Key fact: 180° = π and 360° = 2π. Use these anchors to convert any angle.

slides.title: Right Triangles: The Foundation
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor draws a right triangle. 'This 90° angle is the key. All trig ratios start here.'

points.label: Right angle
points.text: One angle = 90°. The opposite side is the hypotenuse.

points.label: Opposite side
points.text: The side across from the angle you're studying.

points.label: Adjacent side
points.text: The side next to your angle (not the hypotenuse).

points.label: Hypotenuse
points.text: The longest side, opposite the right angle.

example.problem: In a right triangle with angle θ, identify opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse.
example.solution: Label the angle θ. Opposite is across from θ. Adjacent touches θ. Hypotenuse is longest.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every trig ratio compares pairs of sides in a right triangle.

slides.title: Sine, Cosine, and Tangent: The Big Three
slides.storyContext: Arjun draws a right triangle. Mr. Kapoor labels the sides. 'These ratios between sides are the trig functions.'

points.label: tangent θ
points.text: tan θ = opposite / adjacent = sin θ / cos θ.

points.label: Reciprocals
points.text: csc θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ.

example.problem: In a right triangle with opposite = 3, adjacent = 4, hypotenuse = 5. Find sin, cos, tan.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sine, cosine, tangent are ratios of triangle sides.

slides.title: SOH-CAH-TOA: Memory Trick
slides.storyContext: Priya struggles to remember which ratio is which. Arjun teaches: 'SOH-CAH-TOA. SOH = Sine is Opposite/Hypotenuse. CAH = Cosine is Adjacent/Hypotenuse. TOA = Tangent is Opposite/Adjacent.'

slides.title: Applying SOH-CAH-TOA
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor says: 'Use this trick to solve any right triangle problem.'

example.problem: Adjacent side = 5, hypotenuse = 13. Find sin, cos, tan.

slides.inSimpleWords: SOH-CAH-TOA is your map. Pick the ratio you need, then calculate.

slides.title: Unit Circle and Trig for Any Angle
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'What if the angle is 120° or 270°? No right triangle exists.' Mr. Kapoor draws a unit circle. 'The sine and cosine are simply the coordinates of the point.'

points.label: Unit circle
points.text: Circle of radius 1. Point on circle: (cos θ, sin θ).

points.label: For any angle
points.text: cos θ = x-coordinate, sin θ = y-coordinate.

slides.inSimpleWords: The unit circle extends trig functions to all angles using point coordinates.

slides.title: Quadrants and Sign Rules
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor divides the unit circle into four quadrants. 'Q1: all positive. Q2: sin positive. Q3: tan positive. Q4: cos positive. Acronym: ASTC — All Students Take Calculus.'

slides.title: Special Angles: 30°, 45°, 60°
slides.storyContext: Arjun memorizes: '0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° are special. Their trig values come up constantly.'

points.label: Memorization
points.text: Use hand trick or table — values repeat in all quadrants with sign changes.

example.solution: sin 135° = sin 45° = 1/√2 (sine is positive in Q1 and Q2).

slides.inSimpleWords: Memorize 30°, 45°, 60° — they appear constantly in problems.

slides.title: The Hand Trick for Special Angles
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor shows his hand: 'Curl fingers for 0° to 90°. Fingers represent 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° from pinky to thumb. For sin, count fingers below (√count/2). For cos, count above.'

slides.title: Periodicity and Graphs
slides.storyContext: Priya plots sin θ. 'It repeats every 360°!' Mr. Kapoor: 'That's periodicity — sin(θ + 360°) = sin θ.'

points.label: Period of tangent
points.text: tan(θ + π) = tan θ. Period = 180° or π.

slides.inSimpleWords: Trig functions repeat periodically.

slides.title: Temple Height Problem
slides.storyContext: Arjun stands 20 m from temple, angle of elevation is 45°.
slides.inSimpleWords: Set up right triangle, identify known angle and side, use correct ratio, solve.

slides.title: River Width Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun measure angle to a tree: 60° from 50 m away. How wide is the river?

slides.title: Angles of Elevation and Depression
slides.storyContext: Arjun is on a 30 m bridge looking down at Priya. Angle of depression (looking down) and angle of elevation (looking up) are equal.

points.label: Angle of elevation
points.text: Angle above horizontal when looking UP.

points.label: Angle of depression
points.text: Angle below horizontal when looking DOWN.

points.label: Key insight
points.text: Elevation from A = Depression from B (alternate interior angles).

example.problem: From 30 m bridge, angle of depression to boat is 60°. Distance from base?

slides.inSimpleWords: Elevation is looking up; depression is looking down.

slides.title: Real Applications
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor: 'Pilots calculate angle of elevation from ground to sky. When you look up at a building, that angle tells you height relative to distance.'

slides.title: Trigonometric Identities
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor writes key identities: 'These hold for all angles and shortcut harder problems.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Identities relate trig functions; they simplify expressions and solve equations.

slides.title: Two-Angle Building Height
slides.storyContext: From 100 m away, angle of elevation = 30°. Move 50 m closer, angle = 45°. Find height.

example.solution: h₁ = 100/√3 ≈ 57.7 m. h₂ = 50 m. Inconsistent — problem setup wrong. Real problems will match.

slides.inSimpleWords: Set up equations from each angle, solve simultaneously.

slides.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
slides.storyContext: Priya knows opposite = 7, hypotenuse = 10. Find angle θ using inverse sine.

example.problem: Find θ such that sin θ = 7/10.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inverse trig functions find the angle when you know the ratio.

slides.title: Inverse Functions in Navigation
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor: 'In navigation, you know horizontal and vertical distances. You need the angle. Inverse trig functions shine here.'

slides.title: Trigonometric Functions: Key Takeaways

points.text: sin θ = opp/hyp, cos θ = adj/hyp, tan θ = opp/adj.
Unit circle: (cos θ, sin θ); sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Trig functions relate angles to side ratios; solve real-world height/distance problems.

subject: Mathematics
title: Imaginary Treasures: Complex Numbers Unlock Solutions
hook: Not all quadratic equations have real solutions — complex numbers complete the picture.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: Student puzzled by negative square roots

slides.title: The Unsolvable Quadratic
slides.storyContext: Arjun tries x² + 1 = 0, getting x² = −1. He says: 'Square roots of negatives don't exist!' Dr. Patel smiles: 'What if we invent i where i² = −1?'

slides.title: History of the Imaginary Unit
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel: 'For centuries, mathematicians dismissed square roots of negatives. Then Cardano, Euler, Gauss realized: if we invent i where i² = −1, all polynomial equations have solutions.'

slides.title: The Imaginary Unit i
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel defines: 'i satisfies i² = −1. Any number a + bi is a complex number.'

points.label: Complex number
points.text: z = a + bi where a, b ∈ ℝ.

points.label: Imaginary part
points.text: b is the coefficient of i.

slides.inSimpleWords: A complex number is 'real part + imaginary part' using i.

slides.title: Powers of i: A Pattern
slides.storyContext: Arjun calculates: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1, i⁵ = i... 'It repeats every 4!' Priya uses this: i⁹⁹ = i³ = −i since 99 = 4(24) + 3.

slides.title: Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Can we add/subtract complex numbers like real numbers?' Dr. Patel: 'Yes, term by term.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Add real to real, imaginary to imaginary.

slides.title: Multiplication of Complex Numbers
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'How do we multiply?' Dr. Patel: 'FOIL, but remember i² = −1.'

points.label: Multiplication
points.text: (a + bi)(c + di) = ac + adi + bci + bdi² = (ac−bd) + (ad+bc)i.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply like binomials, use i² = −1 to simplify.

slides.title: Why Multiply Complex Numbers?
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'When would we multiply complex numbers?' Dr. Patel: 'In electrical engineering, alternating currents are modeled by complex numbers. Multiplying impedances requires complex multiplication.'

slides.title: Complex Conjugate
slides.storyContext: To divide, Dr. Patel multiplies by the conjugate: if z = a + bi, the conjugate z̄ = a − bi.

points.label: Conjugate
points.text: z = a + bi → z̄ = a − bi.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flip the sign of the imaginary part.

slides.title: Division of Complex Numbers
slides.storyContext: To divide z₁/z₂, multiply by z̄₂/z̄₂.
slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply by conjugate of denominator to rationalize.

slides.title: Modulus and Argument
slides.storyContext: Priya visualizes complex numbers on a plane: real axis horizontal, imaginary axis vertical.

points.label: Argument
points.text: arg(z) = angle θ from positive real axis.

points.label: Polar form
points.text: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r e^(iθ).

slides.inSimpleWords: Modulus is distance from origin; argument is the angle.

slides.title: The Complex Plane
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel draws axes. 'Horizontal is real; vertical is imaginary. Every complex number is a point. Addition becomes vector addition!'

slides.title: Discriminant and Root Types
slides.storyContext: Before solving, Dr. Patel teaches: 'Calculate Δ = b² − 4ac. This tells root types.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The discriminant predicts root type before solving.

slides.title: Quadratic Formula with Complex Roots
slides.storyContext: Arjun solves x² + 2x + 5 = 0. Δ = −16 < 0, so complex solutions exist.
slides.inSimpleWords: When Δ < 0, roots are complex conjugates.

slides.title: Solving 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0
slides.storyContext: Solve and verify solutions.
slides.inSimpleWords: Substitute, simplify radicals, express as a + bi.

slides.title: De Moivre's Theorem
slides.storyContext: Priya raises 1 + i to the 10th power. Using polar form is easier: (r e^(iθ))^n = r^n e^(iθn).

points.label: De Moivre's Theorem
points.text: [r(cos θ + i sin θ)]^n = r^n(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

points.label: nth roots
points.text: nth roots of z: r^(1/n) e^(i(θ+2πk)/n), k=0,1,...,n−1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert to polar, apply theorem, convert back.

slides.title: Complex Numbers in 3D Graphics
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns: 'Video games use complex numbers to rotate objects. Multiplying by e^(iθ) rotates by angle θ. Complex multiplication = rotation + scaling!'

slides.title: Cubic: x³ − 1 = 0
slides.storyContext: One root is x = 1; the other two are complex.

example.problem: Factor and find all three roots.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factor, solve each factor — some yield complex roots.

slides.title: Complex Cube Roots of 8
slides.storyContext: Priya: 'How many cube roots does 8 have?' Dr. Patel: 'In reals, one (2). In complex, three.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Every non-zero complex number has n distinct nth roots.

slides.title: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel concludes: 'Every degree-n polynomial has exactly n roots in the complex numbers. Real numbers alone weren't enough. Complex numbers complete the picture.'

slides.title: Complex Numbers: Key Takeaways

points.text: Add/subtract term-by-term. Multiply using FOIL + i² = −1.
Modulus |z| = √(a²+b²); argument θ from real axis.
De Moivre: [r(cos θ + i sin θ)]^n = r^n(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

slides.inSimpleWords: Complex numbers extend reals; solve all quadratics.

subject: Mathematics
chapterAliases: Linear Inequalities in One and Two Variables
title: Dividing the Market: Linear Inequalities in Budgets and Boundaries
hook: When resources are limited, inequalities define what's possible — not just exact answers.

slides.title: Budgeting for the Festival Stall
slides.storyContext: Arjun runs a fruit stall. He has ₹500 for apples (₹40) and oranges (₹30). Priya: 'How many of each?' Mr. Gupta: 'That's a range of possibilities, not one answer.'

slides.title: Why Inequalities Matter
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta: 'In life, you rarely have exact values. At least ₹500, not exactly. At least 10 kilos. These inequalities define real constraints.'

slides.title: Inequality Symbols
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta writes: x > 5, y ≤ 10. 'Each symbol defines a relationship.'

example.problem: Is x = 5 a solution to x > 3 AND x ≤ 10?

slides.inSimpleWords: An inequality shows a relationship; solve by finding all values making it true.

slides.title: Solving One-Variable Inequalities
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants apples to cost < ₹300: 40x < 300. Priya solves: x < 7.5, so max 7 apples.

points.label: Add/Subtract
points.text: Add or subtract same from both sides; sign stays same.

points.label: Multiply/Divide positive
points.text: Multiply/divide by positive; sign stays same.

points.label: Multiply/Divide negative
points.text: Multiply/divide by negative; FLIP the sign.

slides.inSimpleWords: Solve like equations; flip sign when multiplying/dividing by negatives.

slides.title: The Critical Rule: Negative Flip
slides.storyContext: Arjun forgets and gets it wrong. Priya reminds: 'Multiply by negative? Flip the sign. Example: 5 > 3, but −5 < −3. Negating reverses order!'

slides.title: Multi-Step Solving
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta: 'Solve 2x − 3 ≤ 7.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Step-by-step: isolate variable, apply operations, remember flip rule.

slides.title: Compound Inequalities
slides.storyContext: Arjun: 'I want between 5 and 10 apples' (5 ≤ x ≤ 10). Mr. Gupta: 'Two conditions at once.'

points.label: OR
points.text: At least one true. x < 0 OR x > 10.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compound: two ranges; intervals use parentheses (open) and brackets (closed).

slides.title: Number Line Visualization
slides.storyContext: Priya draws: 'For x ∈ [5, 10], mark 5 with a closed dot (included) and 10 closed. Shade between. For 5 < x < 10, use open dots.'

slides.title: Two-Variable Inequalities
slides.storyContext: Arjun's budget: 40x + 30y ≤ 500. Priya graphs: 'The solution is a region, not a line.'

points.label: Test point
points.text: Test (0,0): 0 ≤ 500? Yes, so shade that region.

example.solution: Dashed line 2x + y = 4. Test (0,0): false, shade NOT containing (0,0).

slides.inSimpleWords: Plot boundary; test point to decide which side; solid or dashed based on symbol.

slides.title: Budget Constraint Graph
slides.storyContext: Arjun has ₹500, wants ≥5 apples, ≥3 oranges. Graph feasible region, find valid point.

example.solution: Boundaries: 40x + 30y = 500, x = 5, y = 3. Valid point: (5, 8) costs ₹440 ≤ ₹500.

slides.inSimpleWords: All constraints as inequalities, plot lines, shade overlap, pick point inside.

slides.title: Systems of Two-Variable Inequalities
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta adds x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (non-negative). Priya: 'Solution is intersection of all regions.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Graph all; solution is where all shading overlaps.

slides.title: Vertices and Optimization
slides.storyContext: Priya notes: 'Vertices matter because the best solution is always at a corner. To maximize profit, check every vertex.'

slides.title: Linear Programming: Objective Function
slides.storyContext: Arjun profits ₹10/apple, ₹8/orange. Maximize P = 10x + 8y subject to constraints.

example.solution: Check vertices: (5,10) → P = 130, (12.5,0) → P = 125. Max at a vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find vertex giving max/min value of objective.

slides.title: Real-World Linear Programming
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta: 'Airlines maximize profit. Factories minimize cost. Hospitals optimize schedules. It's one of math's most powerful tools.'

slides.title: Maximize Profit
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to maximize P = 10x + 8y subject to 40x + 30y ≤ 500, x ≥ 5, y ≥ 3.

example.problem: List all feasible vertices and evaluate P at each.
example.solution: Valid vertices: (5,3)→P=74, (5,10.67)→P=135, (11.67,3)→P=140. Optimal: buy ~12 apples, 3 oranges.

slides.inSimpleWords: Evaluate objective at every vertex; best vertex is optimal.

slides.title: Minimize Cost
slides.storyContext: Priya: minimize C = 40x + 30y with x ≥ 5, y ≥ 3. Cheapest way to meet minimums?

example.solution: Feasible region unbounded. Minimum at closest corner: (5,3). C = ₹290.

slides.inSimpleWords: In minimization, optimal is the corner with smallest objective value.

slides.title: The Simplex Method
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta: 'With 2 variables, we graphed. Real problems have 100s. The Simplex Method finds optimal vertices automatically. It's how the world optimizes.'

slides.title: Linear Inequalities: Key Takeaways

points.text: One-variable: solve like equations; flip sign when multiplying/dividing by negatives.
Compound: combine ranges (AND/OR); write in interval notation.
Two-variable: graph boundary line, shade region, use solid/dashed based on symbol.
Systems: graph all, solution is intersection.
Linear programming: maximize/minimize objective over feasible region; optimal is a vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inequalities describe ranges/regions; systems combine constraints; LP optimizes objectives.
